title: How Bullfighting Works
summary: Josh and Chuck discuss bullfighting (corrida): its history from ancient bull rituals and Visigoth-era horseback bullfighting through the eleventh-century establishment in Spain, royal and aristocratic involvement, and its status as Spain's national sport. They describe the treatment of bulls before the fight, the three acts (tercios) with picadors, banderilleros and the matador, the estocada and descabello killing methods, indultos, famous matadors (Juan Belmonte, Joselito, Manuel Rodriguez "Manolete"), bull breeding, and horse abuse. They cover the decline of bullfighting, including the Catalonia ban effective January 1, 2012, state TV restrictions, government subsidies, and public opinion polls. The episode ends with a comparison to bull baiting and the bulldog's origins, and listener mail about a comics illustrator and a T-shirt design contest.

segments.title: Opening banter and bullfighting intro
segments.summary: Hosts open the show and banter about bullfighting, including Chuck's experience seeing a bullfight in Cancun with tourists, and the idea that tourists keep bullfighting going. They cite rough statistics on bulls killed and matadors killed, and discuss Julio Aparicio's fatal goring and public opinion in Spain.

segments.title: Ancient origins and Visigoth horseback bullfighting
segments.summary: The hosts trace bull rituals to ancient times, including Mycenaean bull-leaping, and describe horseback bullfighting in the Iberian Peninsula under the Visigoths and its survival as rejoneo in Portugal, where bulls are weakened outside the ring.

segments.title: Festivals, running of the bulls and royal and aristocratic history
segments.summary: Bullfighting in Spain is tied to festivals such as the Fiesta de San Fermin in Pamplona, where the running of the bulls began with ranchers moving bulls to the arena. El Cid is named as an early arena bullfighter. Queen Isabella opposed it, Pope Pius V's ban lasted about eight years, and Philip II restricted it to commoners, after which it became the national sport. Royal boxes still exist in some arenas.

segments.title: Pre-fight treatment of bulls
segments.summary: The hosts describe how bulls are handled in the two days before a fight, including being kept in dark boxes, having newspaper placed in their ears, petroleum jelly on their eyes, cotton in nostrils, caustic solution on legs, and being given drugs and laxatives. Chuck pushes back on the account and the hosts discuss whether it is propaganda.

segments.title: The three acts of a bullfight: picadors, banderilleros, matador
segments.summary: The hosts explain the structure of a corrida in three acts, called tercios. Picadors on horseback lance the bull's neck to weaken it, banderilleros place barbed darts, and the matador performs cape work and then kills the bull with a sword thrust (estocada), with a descabello finishing blow if needed. Failed kills, the use of a tractor, and the practice of selling meat afterward are discussed.

segments.title: Indulto, bull reprieves and famous matadors
segments.summary: The hosts describe the indulto, a rare reprieve granted to brave bulls, using the bull Manzanito as an example. They then discuss famous matadors Juan Belmonte and Joselito, Joselito's fatal goring, and Manuel Rodriguez Sanchez (Manolete), who was gored in 1947.

segments.title: Bull breeding, horse abuse and the bullfight business
segments.summary: The hosts discuss that fighting bulls are about four years old, bred on ranches and tested for bravery, and that matadors reportedly request docile bulls. Bulls are rarely used twice. They also describe horses being blindfolded, having ears stuffed and vocal cords severed, and matadors earning large fees per fight.

segments.title: Decline of bullfighting: Catalonia ban, TV and subsidies
segments.summary: The hosts discuss declining popularity, including Catalonia's ban effective January 1, 2012, after the last bullfight in September 2011 in Barcelona. They note a 2010 poll where about 70 percent of Spaniards favored ending it, a state TV coverage restriction, falling fight numbers from about 1,000 to about 200 supported largely by government subsidies, and the Spanish government moving jurisdiction to the cultural ministry. Mexico's consideration of a ban is mentioned.

segments.title: Bull suffering, bull baiting and bulldog origins
segments.summary: The hosts discuss a veterinarian study on bull stress hormones and whether bulls suffer, then compare bullfighting to bear baiting and bull baiting in England, and explain that bulldogs were bred from baiting dogs into a less aggressive breed. Chuck calls for ending ritualized animal killing and asks about culture as a justification.

segments.title: Listener mail: comics code and T-shirt design contests
segments.summary: A listener who is an illustrator writes about the comics episode, including the Comics Code Authority and EC's Mad magazine move. Another listener's note about design contests and T-shirt sales is discussed, and the hosts give contact info for listener mail and their video podcast.

segments.title: Sign-off
segments.summary: The hosts close the episode with a brief sign-off and a reminder of the show's social media and video podcast.
